## Amos 6 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "Woe to those at ease in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria…"

**Traditional Reading (all traditions agree substantially):**

The "woe" opens a funeral dirge form (3-2 beat) used by prophets to express God's disapproval and coming judgment. It addresses the complacent, self-indulgent leaders of both Judah ("Zion") and Israel ("Mount Samaria"). The Hebrew term for "at ease" carries the connotation of "careless, wanton, arrogant" (BDB 983; cf. Isa 32:9,11; Zech 1:15). Their sin is not wealth or leisure itself, but trusting in these things—their fortified capital cities—instead of God. "Distinguished ones" is literally "pierced men"; the Arabic root suggests "one who scrutinizes" (i.e., leaders). The "house of Israel" came to them for judgment and guidance in civil affairs.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-6/
- https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm

**Spurgeon (Baptist) on "at ease":** This is "a carnal ease, a fleshly security … not the confidence of a man who is pardoned, but the ease of a hardened wretch … the ease of a senseless drunkard, whose house is tottering from its sandy foundations." He distinguishes this from the godly rest Jesus offers (Matt 11:28-29) and the rest in Hebrews 4:9-11. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-6/

**Gill (Baptist):** Sees the "woe" as directed at hypocrites in a church state ("Zion"), who trust in external ordinances and church membership, crying "Peace, peace" while destruction is at hand (cf. Matt 25:6, the foolish virgins). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html

**Reformed / Ellicott (Anglican):** Translates "trust" as "the confident (or complacent) dwellers in the mountain of Samaria"—the upper luxurious classes, the rulers. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm

---

### v. 2 — "Cross over to Calneh and see… Are you better than these kingdoms?"

**Traditional Reading:**

Amos challenges Israel to compare themselves to three pagan cities—Calneh (on the Tigris, near Ctesiphon), Hamath the Great (on the Orontes), and Gath of the Philistines—all of which had already fallen or were under threat from Assyria. The point: if these strong cities were not spared, why should Israel think herself immune? Calneh had been destroyed by Tiglath-pileser III around 738 BC. Hamath suffered defeats from Shalmaneser III (~850 BC) and was finally overthrown by Sargon in 720 BC. Gath had been destroyed by Uzziah. — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm

**Gill:** Provides extensive geographical detail, noting Calneh was in the land of Shinar (Gen 10:10), Hamath is "the great" to distinguish it from lesser Hamaths, and Gath was about 14 miles south of Joppa, famous as Goliath's birthplace. He interprets the question as: "Are these kingdoms better than yours? No—therefore you are more ungrateful for sinning against the Lord who gave you such a rich land, and you may expect to fare as they did." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html

**Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** "God wanted to rebuke the pride of Israel by making them compare themselves to some of their pagan neighbors. God wanted them to see that these pagan cities and kingdoms were not so great after all." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-6/

---

### v. 3 — "You dismiss the day of calamity and bring near a reign of violence."

**Traditional Reading:**

The wealthy leaders deliberately put the day of reckoning out of their minds. The Hebrew verb for "put far off" (BDB 622) appears only here in this form. The bitter irony is that by their very acts they were hastening the day of judgment. "Seat of violence" refers to a throne/reign of violence—either the corrupt courts of Israel's leaders, or the coming violent reign of Assyria. Ellicott: "They choose to think that the day of reckoning is far off, and cling yet closer to their habits of defrauding the poor at the seat of judgment." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6

**Gill:** "They endeavoured to put it out of their minds and thoughts, and supposed it to be at a great distance, yea, hoped it never would be; and like the Jews … said it was not near, but prolonged" (cf. Ezek 11:3). He also applies it to those who put far off the day of death and the day of Christ's coming to judgment. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html

---

### v. 4 — "You lie on beds inlaid with ivory… dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall."

**Traditional Reading:**

The ruling class indulges in extreme luxury: beds decorated or inlaid with ivory, sprawling on couches (an unusual—possibly foreign—posture at meals in Palestine at the time), eating only the most delicate, choice meats—lambs picked from the flock and stall-fattened calves. The verb "sprawl" (BDB 710) has a negative connotation and is repeated in v. 7. Gill notes ancient sources attest that the Agrigentines had beds entirely made of ivory (citing Timaeus and Horace). — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm

---

### v. 5 — "You improvise songs on the harp like David and invent your own musical instruments."

**Traditional Reading:**

The Hebrew verb for "improvise" (or "chant") appears only here in the OT; Ellicott renders it "prattle, or jabber." The comparison to David is deeply ironic: David composed songs and made instruments to honor the Lord; these nobles do so purely to entertain themselves at drunken feasts. They "particularized" (as some translations have it)—observing divisions and distinctions of notes by modulating their voices—showing sophisticated but self-indulgent musical culture. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html

**Utley (Baptist/Evangelical):** Suggests the revelers may have been desecrating David's melodies and the instruments used in temple worship. — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6

---

### v. 6 — "You drink wine by the bowlful and anoint yourselves with the finest oils, but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph."

**Traditional Reading:**

They drank not from cups but from large sacrificial basins (the same Hebrew word appears in Exod 38:3 for the bowls used to catch sacrificial blood), indicating excessive drinking. Anointing with fine oil was a sign of festivity and gladness—completely inappropriate given "the ruin of Joseph" (the moral and impending national collapse of the Northern Kingdom, often called "Joseph" for Ephraim and Manasseh). They were "not sick at heart" (Ellicott) for the nation's affliction. Gill notes an allusion to Joseph's brothers who ate while he lay in the pit, and to the chief butler who forgot Joseph amid his cups. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html ; https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6

**Guzik:** "When God makes us prosperous, we have an absolute obligation to use what He gives us in a way that glorifies Him, not that pampers ourselves." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-6/

---

### v. 7 — "Therefore, you will now go into exile as the first of the captives, and your feasting and lounging will come to an end."

**Traditional Reading:**

The punishment fits the sin: those who were "first" in luxury, status, and self-indulgence will be the first dragged into exile. The "banquet" (Hebrew *mirzach*, found only here and Jer 16:5) may refer to a self-indulgent funeral feast—if so, the sarcasm is that their endless partying will become a funeral. Gill notes this was fulfilled when the royal family, princes, nobles, and chief tradesmen were the first carried captive in Jeconiah's captivity (2 Kgs 24:12). Ellicott: "the shout of the loungers (rioting in their banquets) shall cease." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6

---

### v. 8 — "The Lord GOD has sworn by Himself … 'I abhor Jacob's pride and detest his citadels.'"

**Traditional Reading:**

God swears "by Himself" (literally "by His soul") because He can swear by no greater (cf. Heb 6:13). This triple-name declaration ("The Lord GOD … the LORD, the God of Hosts") is an emphasized pronouncement. The rare Hebrew verb for "abhor" (BDB 1060 II) appears only here in the OT and is a powerful term of rejection. "The excellency of Jacob" refers to their pride—their kingdom, wealth, fortified cities, and possibly the shrine at Samaria with its calf-worship. The hatred is not of the buildings as such but of the pride they represented. — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm

**Reformed / JFB:** Sees "the excellency of Jacob" as the temple itself if Judah is included, or the kingdom and fortified cities if limited to Israel. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/amos/6.htm

---

### vv. 9-10 — "If there are ten men left in one house, they too will die… 'Silence … for the name of the LORD must not be invoked.'"

**Traditional Reading:**

These two prose verses (set within poetic context) describe the aftermath of siege and pestilence. "Ten" was the minimum number for a synagogue and for social/military groups in Jewish tradition—yet even this remnant in one house all perish. A near kinsman (uncle on the father's side, or one who burns the bodies) comes to carry out the corpses. Cremation was not the normal Hebrew burial practice (Gen 3:19; burial was standard), but pestilence made it necessary (cf. 1 Sam 31:12, where Saul's body was burned to prevent mockery). The whispered exchange inside the house—"Is anyone else with you?" / "None" / "Silence!"—reflects terror. To mention the LORD's name might draw further wrath. Ellicott suggests the dying man may have begun to curse the Lord or call on Him too late; the relative silences him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html

**Guzik:** "The people would be so terrified at the judgment of God that they would fear to hear even the name of the Lord mentioned" — quoting McComiskey: the survivor "will not permit his mentioning the name of the Lord for fear that the Lord will turn his wrath on him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-6/

**Gill:** The "hold thy tongue" is either to prevent neighbors from being discouraged at the death toll, or to forbid murmuring against God's providence since "it is just and righteous." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html

**Expositor's Bible Commentary:** These verses are "a weird little bit of memory, the recollection of an eye-witness, from one of those great pestilences" of the eighth century. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/amos/6.htm

**Coffman (Church of Christ):** Notes this passage "describes the effects of the famine and pestilence during the siege of Samaria." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/amos-6.html (seen in search excerpt)

---

### v. 11 — "The great house will be smashed to pieces, and the small house to rubble."

**Traditional Reading:**

Judgment falls on all classes—no one escapes. The Hebrew terms for "pieces" and "rubble/fragments" are unusual; the first (used of rain droplets in Song 5:2) means to shatter or grind; the second means to break open like a wall (Ps 141:7). Hubbard (Tyndale OT Commentary) suggests these terms fit an earthquake better than an invasion. — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm

---

### v. 12 — "Do horses gallop on the cliffs? Does one plow the sea with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison…"

**Traditional Reading:**

Two proverbial rhetorical questions, both expecting the answer "No." Horses do not run on rocky crags, and oxen do not plow there (or, by a well-supported textual emendation changing the vowels, "does one plow the sea with oxen?"—which better fits the impossibility theme, as in NRSV, TEV, NJB). The point: Israel has done something equally absurd and unnatural—perverting justice and righteousness into poison (gall/hemlock) and wormwood (bitterness). — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/amos/6.htm

**Calvin (Reformed), quoted in JFB:** "Those that will not be tilled as fields, shall be abandoned as rocks." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/amos/6.htm

**Grotius, quoted in JFB:** "As horses and oxen are useless on a rock, so ye are incapable of fulfilling justice." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/amos/6.htm

**Spurgeon (Baptist), quoted in Guzik:** "Wise men do not send their horses to run upon the rocks; and they do not send their oxen to plough where all their toil would be wasted." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-6/

---

### v. 13 — "You who rejoice in Lo-debar and say, 'Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?'"

**Traditional Reading:**

Lo-debar (meaning "a nothing" or "no word/thing") and Karnaim (meaning "a pair of horns," i.e., strength) were cities in Transjordan captured by Jeroboam II (782-753 BC). Amos uses wordplay: they rejoice in "Nothing" and boast they took "Horns" by their own might. The theological sin is claiming credit for military victories that properly belong to YHWH alone (holy war theology: Exod 13:3,14,16). Ellicott sees "a thing of nought" also as a reference to calf-worship—the idol they trust in is nothing. — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm

**Expositor's Bible Commentary:** "It was just because of this possible play upon their names, that Amos selected these two out of all the recent conquests of Israel." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/amos/6.htm

---

### v. 14 — "For behold, I will raise up a nation against you … from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah."

**Traditional Reading:**

The "nation" is universally identified as Assyria. The geographical description spans the entire Promised Land from the far north (the entrance/pass of Hamath, near the Orontes, Num 34:7-8; Josh 13:5) to the far south (the Brook of the Arabah, likely the Wady el-Ahsa, the southern boundary of Moab, or possibly the Wady el-'Arish if Judah is included). This was the traditional idealized boundary of Israel's territory under Jeroboam II (2 Kgs 14:25)—the very territory they boasted about would be the theater of their affliction. — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html

---

## Denominational Distinctives & Other Views

### Baptist Views

**Spurgeon** (seen throughout Guzik's commentary) emphasizes the distinction between carnal ease and true spiritual rest, the sin of self-indulgence, and the danger of presuming on God's patience. His sermon on this chapter vividly describes the "ease" as that of "a madman, who, because he has hidden his sin from his own eyes, thinks he has concealed it from God" and prays God will break such sleep "or else it will surely bring him where he shall make his bed in hell." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-6/

**Gill** (Particular Baptist, 1746) uniquely spiritualizes "Zion" as the church and "at ease in Zion" as hypocrites who trust in church membership and external ordinances while being spiritually dead (comparing them to the foolish virgins of Matt 25). He reads the verse as applicable to those "never had any true sight of sin, or sense of danger … nor troubled with the temptations of Satan, and have no fears and doubts about their happiness." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/amos-6.html

**Bob Utley (Baptist/Evangelical, bible.org):** Provides a study-guide approach prioritizing the reader's own interpretation alongside the Holy Spirit. His notes emphasize textual and linguistic detail, noting the textual variant in v. 12 ("plow the sea" vs. "plow with oxen") and the possible link of "banqueting" to a funeral feast based on Ugaritic parallels. He emphasizes that Israel's claim to have taken Karnaim "by our own strength" contradicts holy war theology. — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6

### Reformed Views

**Calvin (quoted in JFB):** On v. 12—"Those that will not be tilled as fields, shall be abandoned as rocks," reflecting covenant theology: Israel's failure to produce the fruit of justice renders them like unproductive ground fit only for judgment. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/amos/6.htm

**JFB:** Sees v. 12 as Israel acting "as perversely as if one were to make horses run upon the rock." Also notes Grotius's interpretation: "ye are incapable of fulfilling justice." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/amos/6.htm

**Ligonier (R.C. Sproul's ministry):** In a related devotion on Amos 4, notes: "The issue is never how much money one has but rather what one does with it … God hates it when unrighteous people oppress the poor." Also: "If we do not live a life of repentance, our worship is hollow and displeasing to God." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/limits-gods-patience

### Pentecostal/Charismatic Views

**David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Emphasizes practical application: "When God gives us prosperity and success, we have an absolute obligation to use it to glorify Him and serve others, not to indulge ourselves—because self-indulgence is a sin that invites God's judgment." He carefully distinguishes godly rest (Heb 4:9-11; Rev 14:13) from sinful rest. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-6/

### Anglican View

**Ellicott:** Provides philological and historical detail—the most precise on the Hebrew terms. Notes the ironic contrast between David's holy music and the nobles' self-indulgent "prattling," the use of sacrificial basins for drinking, and the fact that "the excellency of Jacob" in v. 8 may refer to the shrine at Samaria with its calf-worship. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/6.htm

### Church of Christ View

**Coffman:** Emphasizes the "link word" structure: "first" (the distinguished ones are "first of the nations" in v. 1, use the "first/finest" oils in v. 6, and will be "first into captivity" in v. 7). Notes the chapter emphasizes "law and obedience," calling it "the gospel of law, for that, too, is gospel." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/amos-6.html (search excerpt)

### Modern Scholarship (Textual Issue)

**Net Bible / bible.org (Utley):** On v. 12, notes the textual variant "plow the sea" (by changing the vowels of the MT) is adopted by NRSV, TEV, and NJB as fitting the context of impossible acts better than "plow with oxen." The traditional MT reading is retained by NASB, NKJV, ESV. — https://bible.org/seriespage/amos-6
